title: Sufficiency allows ordinary explanation — it denies another divine word or infallible sense-fixer
source_text: XLV. Igitur quamvis Scriptura aliquatenus obscura sit, & apud fideles egeat explicatione, qua ratione jam expositum est, nihil inde concludi potest contra sufficientiam quam Scripturae sacrae tribuimus. Etenim, quum dicimus Scripturam solam sufficere ad fidem & salutem, non intelligimus illam nulla indigere interpretatione, ut inde fideles singuli totam fidei doctrinam hauriant, sed solum ad hoc minime opus esse alio praeter Scripturam Dei verbo, & alia fidei regula, sive interprete quodam infallibili, qui Scripturae sensum alioqui dubium & incertum determinet, & de eo certos nos reddat.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore although Scripture is somewhat obscure, and among the faithful needs explanation, in the way already set out, nothing can thence be concluded against the sufficiency which we attribute to sacred Scripture. For, when we say that Scripture alone suffices for faith and salvation, we do not understand that it needs no interpretation, so that from it individual believers may draw the whole doctrine of faith, but only that for this there is by no means need of another word of God besides Scripture, and another rule of faith, or some infallible interpreter, who determines the otherwise doubtful and uncertain sense of Scripture, and makes us certain of it.
pass_b_english: Some obscurity and need of explanation do not touch Scripture's sufficiency.
Sola Scriptura does not mean every believer needs no help to draw the whole faith alone.
It means: no second divine word, no second faith-rule, no infallible sense-fixer beyond Scripture.
